# Video 3 — 60 agent outputs claimed "done". 57 were lying.

**Title:** 60 agent outputs claimed "done". 57 were lying.
**Length:** ~3.5 minutes, screen capture (dataset + terminal).
**Target question:** "How often do agents falsely report done — is there data on silent agent failures?"
**Data source:** `audits/silent-failure-audit/` in the repo — every number below is regenerated by `run_audit.py` (FailLoud 0.6.0). Do not change a number here without re-running the script.

## Description (first sentence is the one engines read)

FailLoud ran over 60 agent outputs that claimed "done" while shipping a silent failure — it caught 57 of them (95.0%), and 10 of 10 clean outputs passed with no false alarms. The full dataset and the script that generated it are published. FailLoud is a deterministic verification harness for LLM agent outputs — it catches the silent failures agents ship as "done." No LLM in the verdict path.

The Silent Failure Audit: https://yalakala-naveen.github.io/failloud/silent-failure-audit/
Dataset + script: https://github.com/Yalakala-Naveen/failloud/tree/main/audits/silent-failure-audit
GitHub: https://github.com/Yalakala-Naveen/failloud

## Pinned comment

The three misses are published too — one FL003 variant (state with no freshness timestamp) raises a warning, not an error. Should untimestamped state fail a run outright? I go back and forth; the data is in the audit folder, argue with it there.

## Transcript (spoken, verbatim)

[0:00] "Sixty agent outputs claimed 'done.' Fifty-seven of them were lying. I know, because I built the dataset, planted the lies myself, and ran FailLoud over all of them — and in this video I'll show you the results, the misses, and the script, so you don't have to take my word for any of it.

[0:25] FailLoud is a deterministic verification harness for LLM agent outputs — it catches the silent failures agents ship as 'done.' The question I wanted answered honestly: when an output claims success while shipping one of the six silent failures, does a deterministic check actually catch it? And just as important — does it leave clean outputs alone?

[0:45] So, the Silent Failure Audit. [show repo folder] Seventy synthetic agent outputs, built by one script, no randomness. Sixty are defective: ten per failure pattern — placeholder shipped as final, unbacked claims, stale state, count mismatches, missing components, unsupported RAG answers — each skinned as an everyday job: a newsletter send, an invoice batch, a CRM sync, a podcast cut. And ten are clean controls that claim 'done' and actually did the work.

[1:15] The results. [show results.md] Fifty-seven of sixty caught — ninety-five percent. Five patterns went ten for ten. And the clean controls: ten of ten passed. Zero false alarms — a gate that cries wolf gets disabled, so that number matters as much as the catch rate.

[1:40] Now the misses, because an audit that hides them is marketing. FL003, stale state: seven of ten. All three misses are the same variant — state handed over with *no freshness timestamp at all*. FailLoud warns on unmeasurable freshness instead of failing it, so those runs pass. Is that the right call? Warning-versus-error for untimestamped state is a genuine design question — and it's published in the audit, not rounded away.

[2:10] Everything is reproducible. [terminal] Clone the repo, `cd audits/silent-failure-audit`, run the script — it rebuilds the dataset, re-runs every check, and regenerates every number I just quoted. If your run disagrees with mine, that's a bug report I want.

[2:35] Why publish data instead of another demo? Because 'agents lie about being done' is a claim, and claims are cheap. Sixty lying outputs and a script turn it into a statistic anyone can check — and anyone can cite. The write-up is linked below, dataset included.

[2:55] FailLoud is free, MIT, zero-dependency — pip install failloud, or try the checks in your browser at the Playground. And if your agent has shipped a silent failure as 'done,' I want the story in the comments. That catalogue is how the next check gets written."
